spots.name: Huaca Pucllana
spots.label: Huaca Pucllana

text.access_note: This is a ticketed archaeological site with its own rules on photography, so check the official site before you go.
text.description:
Huaca Pucllana is a huge stepped pyramid of adobe and clay in the middle of Miraflores, built from seven staggered platforms. It was a ceremonial and administrative centre of the Lima Culture, who lived on the central coast of Peru between about 200 and 700 AD. The enclosure is over 500 metres long, 100 metres wide and 22 metres high. The site museum opened in 1984.

It photographs well because the pyramid is built from rows of small bricks, which catch strong light and throw sharp shadows across the walls. Modern apartment blocks rise right behind it, so you can show an ancient structure inside a busy city. The best-known shot is the pyramid lit up at night, taken from the visitor paths or the restaurant side. Lights and shadows then play across the brickwork.

For the evening shot, arrive around sunset and stay into the evening, before the lights go off. This is about 10:30 pm, but the timing may change. Keep your phone steady against a wall or rail and let it take its time in low light. For a different view, stand on Calle General Borgoño and frame the yellow entrance façade with the site name, the pyramid's adobe face and the street traffic. Check the official site before you go, for entry and photography rules.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head to General Borgoño (block 8) in Miraflores. The entrance is on that street. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the site itself, so there is no further walk to the subject. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Huaca Pucllana is in the Miraflores district of central Lima, on General Borgoño (block 8). The pyramid sits right among the apartment blocks and streets of the neighbourhood.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the stepped edges of the platforms level with them. Put the pyramid in the lower two-thirds and leave the sky above it. Include a bit of path or wall in front to give a sense of scale. For the street view, line up the yellow façade with the pyramid wall behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole pyramid with the lights on it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the entrance side to fit in the façade, the adobe wall and the street. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the brick rows and the light and shadow on them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From the site's visitor paths or the restaurant side you can shoot the illuminated pyramid before dinner, with strong light and shadow across the adobe bricks. As an alternative, a second view shows the stepped pyramid in the foreground with Miraflores apartment blocks behind it. Another is from Calle General Borgoño, for the yellow entrance façade with the pyramid's adobe face and street traffic in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone still against a rail or wall until the shot finishes. Tap the brightest part of the pyramid to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the lit bricks don't turn pale.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset and into the evening, before the lights are turned off. This is about 10:30 pm, but it may change.

spots.alt: Huaca Pucllana, Lima: a huge stepped pyramid of adobe and clay in the middle of Miraflores. Photo spot

spots.name: Larco Museum
spots.label: Larco Museum

text.access_note: This is a privately owned museum, so entry is likely to be ticketed and photography rules may apply inside; check the official site before you go.
text.description:
The Larco Museum is a privately owned museum of pre-Columbian art in the Pueblo Libre district of Lima. It is housed in an 18th-century vice-royal building, so the setting is as much a part of the picture as the collection. Its galleries give a chronological tour of about 5,000 years of Peruvian history, and it is especially well known for its gallery of pre-Columbian erotic pottery. There is also a Gold and Silver Gallery with crowns, earrings, masks and other ornaments worked in gold.

The collection began in 1925, when Rafael Larco Herrera acquired around 600 ceramic pieces. His son, Rafael Larco Hoyle, built it up, and the museum first opened to the public on 28 July 1926, Peru's Independence Day.

For photographers, the appeal is the mix of old building and carefully lit objects. Outside, step back far enough to take in the building's lines, then move in for details such as doorways, walls and plants. Inside, display cases are the main subject: ceramics and gold ornaments make strong close-ups when you fill the frame with one object. Reflections in the glass are the usual problem, so angle yourself slightly off to one side rather than shooting straight on. Rules on photography inside galleries can differ from room to room, so look out for signs and ask staff if unsure.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check a map app for the route to Museo Larco in Pueblo Libre. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: The Larco Museum is in the Pueblo Libre district of Lima, in an 18th-century vice-royal building.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight to avoid a leaning look. Outside, fill the frame with one feature such as a doorway or a section of wall. Inside, shoot one object at a time and stand slightly off-centre to the case to avoid your own reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of the building and the display cases. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for tight courtyards or to fit more of the façade in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details on ceramics and gold pieces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Frame the exterior from wherever visitors can stand, then go inside for the collection.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the object to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so gold and bright pieces keep their detail against dark backgrounds. Keep the flash off, as it bounces off glass. Hold the phone steady against your body, since a tripod is unlikely to be allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside, daylight hours give the cleanest views of the building. Inside, lighting is fixed, so time of day matters less; going earlier or at a quieter moment gives you clearer access to the cases.

spots.name: Larcomar
spots.label: Larcomar

text.access_note: The mall has its own access hours and some terraces may be for restaurant customers only at times, so check the official site before you go; the open-air terraces are free to walk into, though a drink or meal is often expected if you want a seat.
text.description: Larcomar is a shopping centre built into the cliff edge in Miraflores, with open-air terraces stepping down towards the Pacific. It photographs well because the whole coastline opens up in front of you: sea, cliffs and, on a clear evening, the sky changing colour above the water. The terrace facing San Lorenzo Island is the classic postcard angle, and from there the frame shows the Pacific coastline, the cliffs and the island. The centre opened on 27 November 1998 and was designed by architect Eduardo Figari Gold. You reach it through Alfredo Salazar Park, which also has a scenic overlook, a children's playground and a few monuments, including a statue of Paddington Bear added in 2015. The terrace is popular, so arrive early if you want a spot at the railing, ideally about an hour before sunset. Start with a wide shot that includes the cliffs and the water, then move in on smaller details: the island, the lines of the cliffs, people at the rail. Keep your lens clean, because sea air can leave a haze on it. If you have time afterwards, Parque del Amor along the coast is a separate sunset photo spot with the El Beso sculpture.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Miraflores and walk or take a taxi to the junction of José Larco Avenue and the Malecón de la Reserva. Walk into Alfredo Salazar Park, which leads to the centre. The phone icon on the map is at Larcomar itself, so once you are inside there is no further walk to the viewpoint. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Larcomar is in Miraflores District, in Alfredo Salazar Park where José Larco Avenue meets the Malecón de la Reserva. It sits on the cliff edge, directly across the street from the JW Marriott Hotel Lima.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the top or bottom line so the sea or the sky fills most of the frame. Include a curve of the cliff edge or the terrace railing in the foreground for depth. Keep the horizon level, because it is obvious over open water. Parque del Amor, with the El Beso sculpture, is an alternative if you want a different sunset setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main terrace view, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more cliff and coastline into the frame. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out San Lorenzo Island or details along the shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the open-air terrace at Larcomar facing San Lorenzo Island and the Pacific. From here the view shows the Pacific coastline, the cliffs and San Lorenzo Island. If the terrace is full, Parque del Amor along the coast is a second option, a separate sunset photo spot with the El Beso sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or sea to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. After the sun has gone, try night mode and brace your phone on the railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About an hour before sunset, which also helps you get a place at the railing before it fills up.

spots.alt: Larcomar, Lima: a shopping centre built into the cliff edge in Miraflores. Photo spot
